note: What `ShellBridge.bootstrapScript` puts on `window.shell` (BRIDGE.md §3), and the detection rule the web side applies to it. `injected` lists *values*, not the functions; `methods` is what decides which functions exist, and `capabilities` is informational — presence of the method is the only gate.

updateReady.note: How the shell tells a running page that a new bundle is verified and staged (BRIDGE.md §5, §7). Not a bridge method: the page does not ask, it is told, so the shell only has to `evaluateJavascript` a dispatch. Both spellings land on the same notice; the event is the one a plugin can also subscribe to. Purely informational — promotion happens at the next launch either way. It lives here because the listeners shipped on the web side before anything in the shell fired them, and a shared string is what keeps the two halves from drifting apart silently.

detection.name: a string is not a bridge
an object claiming no version is not a bridge
a version that is not a number is not a bridge
the BRIDGE.md spelling alone is accepted
detection.note: `version` is what the committed kernel reads and `bridgeVersion` is the name this document uses; the shell injects both and the kernel accepts either.

detection.name: a shell newer in major degrades rather than guesses
detection.note: An old bundle on a new shell ignores the bridge entirely and uses browser fallbacks (BRIDGE.md §8). It still works; it just gets no native behaviour.

detection.name: a serverBaseUrl that is not an absolute http(s) URL is ignored
detection.note: window.shell is reachable by full-trust plugin code, so the value is validated rather than trusted; falling back to the page origin is a working answer in a browser and a safe one everywhere.

detection.name: a trailing slash is stripped so callers can concatenate a rooted path
